claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has a single-phase BCC structure.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has high density.
The baseline alloy has low room-temperature ductility, with fracture strain below 10%.
A minor Si addition to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce a C15 Laves phase such as Hf-Mo-Si.
The Si-induced C15 Laves phase will form a reticulated network within the BCC matrix.
Si addition can trigger spinodal decomposition or precipitation of a secondary intermetallic phase in this alloy.
A reticulated Laves-phase network will impede cracks by crack deflection, branching, and bridging.
A continuous BCC matrix will provide ductility while the hard intermetallic phase provides strengthening.
A continuous ordered B2 matrix in Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr produced high strength but poor room-temperature compressive ductility.
C15 Laves-phase precipitation has been observed at elevated deposition temperature in an Hf-Nb-Ti-V-Zr alloy.
Formation of a C15 Laves phase can increase hardness relative to a single-phase BCC state.
The Si-modified alloy will have yield strength comparable to or higher than the baseline because of precipitation hardening.
The Si-modified alloy will exceed 15% total strain at room temperature.
The Si addition and formation of the proposed Laves phase will slightly increase alloy density.
The Si-modified alloy will have a better room-temperature strength-ductility synergy than the baseline.
Hf and Mo are present in quantities sufficient to form Laves phases in the proposed baseline alloy.
Keeping the Si content low will prevent formation of a continuous brittle intermetallic matrix.
Annealing at 800°C for 24 hours will ensure phase equilibrium in the Si-modified Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys.

contradictions.description: The desired Laves phase is described as a continuous reticulated network, while the boundary condition warns against a continuous brittle phase. The distinction between a permissible continuous network and an impermissible continuous intermetallic matrix is not operationally defined.

The rule states that simultaneous decreases in strength and ductility would indicate that Si acts solely as a solid-solution strengthener, even though a decrease in strength is not consistent with the stated strengthening role.
